items.title: The order list returns each order's city and country as entered at checkout
covers: AC1: city and country as entered at checkout
AC2: each order's own address

items.title: The order list keeps every existing field with its name and value

items.title: My orders shows a "Ships to" column with the order's city and country
covers: AC1: Ships to heading with city and country
Decisions: City, Country between Date and Total

items.title: Two orders with different addresses each show their own city and country
covers: AC2: each row shows its own order's city and country

A rendering bug that repeats the first row's destination or mixes rows up would pass TC-SHIP-1-03 with a single order, so this case needs two orders with different cities and different countries, checked row by row in the browser.

items.title: A shopper with no orders sees the unchanged empty state
covers: AC3: no orders looks exactly as today

The empty-state branch is rendered only by the real page, so it is checked in the browser with the seeded `bob`, who has no orders in scenario `default`.

items.title: Number, date, total and status columns show the same values as before
covers: AC4: order number, date, total and status show exactly what they show today
items.reason: AC4 guards against the new column shifting or corrupting the existing ones (for example the total moving under the wrong header or the status badge losing its class). TC-SHIP-1-02 proves the API still returns the values; this case proves the page still renders them in their own cells. It needs a real placed order, so it runs in the browser on the test stack.

items.title: At phone width a long city name is fully readable and the page does not scroll sideways
covers: AC5: Ships to readable at phone width, no sideways scroll
Decisions: value wraps (overflow-wrap anywhere, min-width 0)
items.reason: AC5 is a layout requirement that only a rendered page at a phone viewport can prove. A short city fits anywhere, so the case uses a real, very long single-word city name: without wrapping it is exactly what would force a horizontal scroll or be clipped. This is the boundary of "stays readable".

subject: SHIP-1
reason: Council (testPlan, blockOn any, pass 9/10): not passed; opus 7/10, sol 8/10; 2 finding(s) stand, 1 note(s).

items.reason: 'Stays readable' is not asserted in a way that can fail: a cell that breaks after every letter still has no horizontal scroll, sits inside the viewport, has scrollWidth <= clientWidth and its full textContent. The only data is one unbreakable 58-letter city, so the case never shows that ordinary values wrap only between words. Add an order shipping to 'Redmond, U.S.' and assert at 375x667 that its .order-ships-to is as wide as its row (within 1px) and renders on one line (height not above 1.5x the computed line-height). For the long-city order, assert the cell is as wide as its row and 'United Kingdom' is not broken mid-word.

The assertions prove that text fits without clipping, but a one-character-wide cell wrapping after every letter satisfies all of them. Add a 375px check using Redmond, U.S. and assert that the rendered destination occupies at most two lines, as required by the upheld ui-ships-to-375-unreadable finding. Keep the long-word overflow check.

'Shows the recorded date (same day and time, in the format My orders already uses)' does not say the exact expected text, so two engineers would write different date assertions. Orders.razor:46 renders @order.Date with DateTime.ToString() in the WebApp's culture. Name the expected text, e.g. the recorded API date converted the way the WebApp converts it and formatted with the WebApp's culture to the second, or say it is the string the WebApp renders for that DateTime.

subject: SHIP-1
reason: Council (testAutomation, blockOn any, pass 9/10): not passed; opus 9/10, sol 8/10; 3 finding(s) stand, 1 note(s).

items.reason: The recorded response shows Redmond/U.S. as order 10 and Paris/France as order 1, contradicting the case's lower-number/higher-number expectations. The test correlates each order using the newly added ID instead. Correct the plan to record each POST's added orderNumber and assert destinations by those IDs, as TC-SHIP-1-04 does; numeric ordering cannot identify creation order here.

The case requires date to be no later than the GET time, but the assertion accepts getTime + 1000 milliseconds. A future timestamp within that extra second passes. Enforce the specified upper bound or obtain an explicit clock-tolerance requirement in the plan.

The test accepts any status later in STATUS_SEQUENCE without checking that the order actually reached it. For a recorded Submitted order, a UI incorrectly displaying Paid, Shipped or Cancelled passes. When the displayed status differs, verify it against the real order state through the API.

Expected result says the item with the lower orderNumber is order A (Redmond) and the higher is order B (Paris). Order numbers come from a HiLo sequence and are not ordered by creation: the recorded run shows Redmond=10 and Paris=1. The test (correctly) identifies each order by the orderNumber recorded when it was placed. The case should say 'the item whose orderNumber is the one recorded for order A/B' instead of lower/higher.

subject: SHIP-1
reason: Council (testPlan, blockOn any, pass 9/10): passed; opus 9/10, sol 10/10; 0 finding(s) stand, 2 note(s).

items.reason: The date expectation compares the API 'date' with host-clock times T0 and GET time, but does not say how to interpret a date without an offset (the API returns none; the spec assumes UTC) and allows no tolerance for the container clock running ahead of the host, while the test applies CLOCK_SKEW_MS (e2e/teststack/ship-1.spec.ts:184), so plan and test disagree. State that a zone-less date is UTC and either give an explicit clock-skew tolerance on the upper bound or keep the bound strict and have the test follow it.

'or a later status the order has reached' does not say how the later status is confirmed, so a UI that shows a wrong status could pass. Specify: if the shown status differs from the recorded one, it must equal the status from a fresh GET /api/orders?api-version=1.0 as alice made after the page loads.
